drafts.title: Hypothetical Batching Tradeoff: Throughput vs. Latency in Local LLM Inference
drafts.body: This post explores a hypothetical scenario regarding batching strategies for local LLM inference. We're examining an experiment where a batch size of 1 yielded an aggregate throughput of 22 tokens per second. In contrast, increasing the batch size to 4 hypothetically resulted in a higher aggregate throughput of 55 tokens per second (F1, F2). It's crucial to understand that these figures are purely illustrative and not actual measured results (F4). Furthermore, the experiment did not measure per-request latency, focusing solely on aggregate throughput (F3). This suggests a potential tradeoff: larger batches may increase overall system capacity but could also impact the responsiveness for individual requests, though this latency aspect was not directly evaluated here. Further investigation would be needed to confirm these hypothetical observations and measure latency.
drafts.plan: This draft focuses on presenting the hypothetical batching tradeoff, emphasizing the aggregate throughput increase with larger batch sizes while clearly stating the limitations regarding per-request latency and the synthetic nature of the data.

drafts.title: Exploring Hypothetical LLM Batching: Aggregate Throughput Gains and Unmeasured Latency
drafts.body: We are considering a hypothetical experiment investigating the impact of batch size on local LLM inference performance. The scenario posits that a batch size of 1 achieved an aggregate throughput of 22 tokens per second. When this batch size was hypothetically increased to 4, the aggregate throughput rose to 55 tokens per second (F1, F2). It is important to note that these numbers are for illustrative purposes only and do not represent real-world test results (F4). This hypothetical experiment did not include measurements for per-request latency (F3). The observed increase in aggregate throughput with larger batches suggests a potential benefit for high-load scenarios. However, the lack of latency measurements means we cannot infer how this batching strategy might affect the responsiveness for individual inference requests. These are hypothetical findings, and actual performance may vary.
